triage.name: Diabetic Foot
triage.reason: Ulcer with neuropathy and vascular disease; rich history, exam and imaging workup with infection and osteomyelitis differential.

review_issues: presentation: older format without SNOMED terms
exam: older format without SNOMED terms

demographics: More common in men than women
More common in Black, Hispanic, and Native American populations, reflecting higher rates of diabetes and its complications
More common in people with lower income and less access to routine foot care
More common in regions with higher diabetes prevalence

risk_factors.text: Peripheral neuropathy with loss of protective sensation
Peripheral arterial disease or prior lower-extremity revascularization
Foot deformity (Charcot foot, hammer toes, prominent metatarsal heads, bunions)
Calluses, corns, or dry cracked skin

family_history: Diabetes mellitus in a first-degree relative
social_history: Limited access to routine foot care or podiatry
Low health literacy or difficulty performing daily foot checks
exposures: Heat or cold exposure to the feet (heaters, hot water bottles, walking on hot surfaces)

chief_complaints.text: There's a sore on my foot that won't heal
My feet feel numb and tingly
I didn't even know I had a wound until I saw it
My foot is red, warm, and swollen
There's a bad smell coming from my foot

hpi.onset: Gradual; a wound that may have started days to weeks earlier, often unnoticed because of numbness
hpi.duration: Usually days to weeks, sometimes months for a chronic ulcer
hpi.progression: Slowly enlarging wound that fails to heal; may become infected, drain pus, or turn black if blood flow is poor
hpi.location: Most often the plantar surface of the foot under the metatarsal heads or the heel; also toes, between toes, or over bony prominences
hpi.radiation: Pain, if present, may radiate up the leg; numbness is usually in a stocking distribution
hpi.quality: Painless or minimally painful open sore; burning, tingling, or sharp shooting pains from neuropathy; deep aching if infection or ischemia is present
hpi.severity: Variable; often painless because of neuropathy, but can be severe if infection or ischemia develops
hpi.timing: Constant wound; neuropathic pain often worse at night
aggravating: Bearing weight on the affected foot

associated_symptoms.text: Numbness or loss of feeling in the feet
Tingling or burning in the feet
Callus or thickened skin near the wound
Drainage or pus from the wound
Redness, warmth, or swelling of the foot
Black or dead tissue at the wound edges
Shaking chills or feeling very unwell

pertinent_negatives: Severe pain out of proportion to the wound
Rapidly spreading redness or streaks up the leg
Sudden onset of a hot, swollen joint
History of a tick bite or rash
Recent trauma with an open fracture
Claudication that resolves completely with rest and no wound

argues_against: Systemic illness without a foot source

positives.text: Dry, cracked skin on the feet
Redness or warmth around the wound

argues_against: Primary dermatologic condition causing the wound

positives.text: Swelling of the foot or ankle

argues_against: Primary arthritis or acute crystal arthropathy

positives.text: Burning pain in the feet, worse at night
Loss of balance or unsteady walking

negatives: Sudden weakness on one side of the body
Loss of bowel or bladder control

positives.text: Leg pain with walking that goes away with rest

negatives: Swelling in both legs up to the knees
argues_against: Heart failure as the cause of leg swelling
Thyroid disease as the cause of neuropathy

atypical.how_it_differs: May present with a painless, deep ulcer and little or no fever despite serious infection; confusion or falls may be the first sign.
More severe neuropathy and vascular calcification; wounds heal poorly and infection risk is higher.
Blunted inflammatory response with minimal redness, warmth, or pus despite deep infection.
Increased pressure on the plantar foot and difficulty seeing or reaching the feet, so wounds are found later.

general.mild: Well-appearing, ambulatory, in no distress; may be unaware of the wound
general.moderate: Uncomfortable, limping or favoring the foot, but not toxic-appearing
general.severe: Ill-appearing, febrile, reluctant to bear weight, foot swollen and draining
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, diaphoretic, confused or lethargic, with spreading infection or gangrene

findings.maneuver: Inspect the entire foot, including the plantar surface, between the toes, and the heel
findings.finding: Open ulcer, most often over a metatarsal head or the heel, with callus at the margins

findings.maneuver: Test sensation with a 10-g monofilament at multiple plantar sites, plus vibration with a 128-Hz tuning fork and pinprick
findings.finding: Reduced or absent protective sensation in a stocking distribution

findings.maneuver: Palpate the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses
Gently probe the ulcer base with a sterile blunt probe
Inspect and palpate the skin around the wound
findings.finding: Erythema, warmth, and induration extending from the ulcer

findings.maneuver: Inspect and gently express the wound
Palpate the soft tissues of the foot and leg
findings.finding: Crepitus or gas in the tissues, suggesting necrotizing infection

findings.maneuver: Inspect the toes and wound edges
findings.finding: Black, dry or wet necrotic tissue (gangrene)

findings.maneuver: Inspect the foot for bony prominences, hammer toes, and Charcot changes
findings.finding: Foot deformity with prominent metatarsal heads or rocker-bottom midfoot

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin of both feet
Assess the affected joint for swelling, warmth, and range of motion
findings.finding: No acute monoarticular swelling or hot joint

findings.maneuver: Inspect the leg for ascending erythema or lymphangitic streaking
findings.finding: No erythema or tenderness extending above the ankle

labs.caveat: A normal white count does not exclude a deep foot infection, especially in older or immunocompromised patients.
Nonspecific; useful mainly when osteomyelitis is suspected.
Rises early in infection and falls with treatment; helps track response.
Supports a bacterial cause and systemic involvement but does not localize the infection.
Infection worsens hyperglycemia; poor control impairs wound healing.
Reflects chronic glycemic control and risk of poor healing.
Diabetic nephropathy is common; affects antibiotic dosing.
Rises with dehydration and renal impairment.
Low albumin predicts poor wound healing and higher amputation risk.
Elevation suggests systemic sepsis or necrotizing infection and warrants urgent surgical evaluation.
Prolonged in malnutrition, liver disease, or with warfarin.

imaging.preferred_when: First-line imaging for any diabetic foot ulcer or suspected bone infection

findings.text: Soft tissue swelling and loss of the normal soft tissue planes
Cortical erosion or periosteal reaction at the ulcer margin
Focal lucency or mottled bone destruction suggesting osteomyelitis
Gas in the soft tissues
Vascular calcification of the foot arteries
Bone destruction, subluxation, or a rocker-bottom deformity suggesting Charcot foot
Normal-appearing bone early in osteomyelitis (plain films lag 10 to 14 days)

imaging.study: MRI of the foot without and with IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Suspected osteomyelitis when plain films are negative or nondiagnostic, or to plan surgery

findings.text: Bone marrow edema with low signal on T1 and high signal on fluid-sensitive sequences
Bone marrow enhancement after contrast
Adjacent soft tissue abscess or sinus tract extending to bone
Cortical destruction and periosteal reaction
Reactive marrow edema from a nearby ulcer without true infection (false positive)

imaging.preferred_when: When MRI is contraindicated or unavailable

findings.text: Focally increased radiotracer uptake on all three phases in the region of the ulcer
Diffusely increased uptake from Charcot or recent surgery (false positive)

imaging.study: Labeled leukocyte scan with or without SPECT/CT
imaging.preferred_when: When osteomyelitis is suspected but MRI or bone scan is equivocal, especially with Charcot foot

findings.text: Focal accumulation of labeled leukocytes in bone, indicating infection

imaging.study: Arterial duplex ultrasound of the lower extremities
imaging.preferred_when: Assessing peripheral arterial disease when pulses are diminished or the ulcer is not healing

findings.text: Focal stenosis or occlusion in the tibial or pedal arteries
Dampened or monophasic Doppler waveforms distal to a stenosis
Diffuse calcification of the arterial wall

imaging.study: CT angiography of the lower extremities
imaging.preferred_when: Planning revascularization when duplex is inconclusive and renal function permits contrast

findings.text: Multilevel arterial stenoses or occlusions in the femoropopliteal and tibial vessels
Heavy medial arterial calcification
Distal runoff vessels suitable for bypass or angioplasty

imaging.study: CT of the foot without contrast
imaging.preferred_when: When MRI is contraindicated and bone detail is needed

findings.text: Cortical destruction and sequestrum formation in osteomyelitis
Soft tissue gas or abscess

initial.why: Looks for leukocytosis and anemia; guides severity assessment
Assesses renal function, electrolytes, and glucose before antibiotics and possible surgery
Hyperglycemia impairs healing and worsens infection
Documents chronic glycemic control and healing prognosis
First-line imaging for any diabetic foot ulcer; looks for osteomyelitis, gas, and Charcot changes

initial.test: Wound culture from deep tissue or curettage
initial.why: Identifies the pathogen and guides antibiotic choice
initial.only_if: infection is suspected (purulent drainage, erythema, or systemic signs)

initial.test: Arterial duplex ultrasound of the lower extremities
initial.why: Assesses perfusion when pulses are diminished or the ulcer is not healing
initial.only_if: peripheral arterial disease is suspected (absent pulses, claudication, or a nonhealing ulcer)

confirmatory.test: MRI of the foot without and with IV contrast
confirmatory.why: Most accurate test for osteomyelitis when plain films are negative or equivocal
confirmatory.only_if: osteomyelitis is suspected (probe-to-bone, visible bone, or a deep nonhealing ulcer)

confirmatory.test: Bone biopsy with histology and culture
confirmatory.why: Definitive diagnosis of osteomyelitis and the only reliable way to identify the causative organism
confirmatory.only_if: osteomyelitis is suspected and the diagnosis remains uncertain or the patient is not responding to antibiotics

supporting.why: Tracks the inflammatory response and treatment effect
Supports the diagnosis of bone infection and monitors response
Helps distinguish bacterial infection and systemic involvement
supporting.only_if: sepsis or a deep infection is a concern

supporting.why: Screens for sepsis or necrotizing infection
supporting.only_if: systemic signs are present (fever, hypotension, tachycardia, or confusion)

supporting.why: Low values predict poor wound healing and higher amputation risk
Alternative when MRI is contraindicated or unavailable

supporting.test: Labeled leukocyte scan with or without SPECT/CT
supporting.why: Helps separate osteomyelitis from Charcot foot when other imaging is equivocal
supporting.only_if: Charcot foot is present or MRI is equivocal

supporting.test: CT angiography of the lower extremities
supporting.only_if: revascularization is being planned and renal function permits contrast

supporting.why: Assesses coagulation before debridement or amputation
supporting.only_if: surgery is planned or the patient takes warfarin

supporting.why: Assesses coagulation before debridement or amputation
supporting.only_if: surgery is planned or the patient takes warfarin

not_indicated.why: No role in the evaluation of a diabetic foot ulcer or infection
Not needed unless abdominal pain suggests pancreatitis
Not part of the acute foot workup; neuropathy is usually diabetic
Not routinely needed unless a urinary infection is suspected

not_indicated.test: CT of the foot without contrast
not_indicated.why: Inferior to MRI for osteomyelitis and not routinely needed

decision_points: Assess perfusion early: absent pulses or a nonhealing ulcer should prompt vascular imaging and revascularization referral
Probe the ulcer to bone and obtain plain films; if osteomyelitis is suspected and films are negative, proceed to MRI
Obtain deep tissue culture, not a superficial swab, before starting antibiotics when infection is present
Look for systemic signs (fever, hypotension, tachycardia, confusion) and elevated lactate, which suggest sepsis or necrotizing infection and need urgent surgical debridement
Check renal function before contrast imaging and adjust antibiotic doses accordingly

differential.name: Osteomyelitis
differential.why_considered: A deep diabetic foot ulcer can extend to bone, and infection of the underlying bone is the main complication that changes management.
differential.trigger: A deep or nonhealing ulcer, visible bone, or a probe that reaches bone

history: Ulcer present for weeks to months despite offloading
Persistent or worsening pain even at rest
Prior foot infection or amputation
exam: Visible bone in the wound base
Ulcer over a bony prominence with surrounding cellulitis
labs: Leukocytosis (may be normal in chronic infection)
imaging: Cortical erosion, periosteal reaction, or focal lucency on plain films
Bone marrow edema with low T1 and high fluid-sensitive signal on MRI
Focal labeled leukocyte uptake in bone

differential.name: Necrotizing soft tissue infection
differential.why_considered: A diabetic foot infection can spread rapidly through the deep fascia and is a surgical emergency.
differential.trigger: Pain out of proportion to the wound, rapidly spreading erythema, crepitus, or systemic toxicity

history: Rapid progression over hours to days
Severe pain despite a small wound
Feeling very unwell with fever and chills
exam: Crepitus or gas in the tissues
Skin anesthesia or dusky, bullous, or necrotic skin
imaging: Soft tissue gas on plain films or CT
Fascial thickening and fluid tracking on MRI or CT

differential.name: Peripheral arterial disease with ischemic ulcer
differential.why_considered: Poor perfusion alone can cause a nonhealing foot wound and mimics an infected diabetic ulcer.

history: Claudication or rest pain
Painful ulcer, often worse at night
Smoking history
exam: Absent dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses
Ulcer at the toe tips or over the lateral malleolus
labs: Elevated A1c and creatinine reflecting chronic vascular risk
imaging: Focal tibial or pedal artery stenosis or occlusion on duplex

differential.name: Charcot neuroarthropathy
differential.why_considered: A warm, swollen, erythematous foot in a patient with neuropathy can be mistaken for infection.

history: Gradual swelling without an open wound
No fever or systemic symptoms
Long-standing diabetes with severe neuropathy
exam: Warm, swollen foot with intact skin
labs: Normal or only mildly elevated inflammatory markers
imaging: Bone destruction, subluxation, or fracture on plain films
Marrow edema on MRI without a sinus tract to bone

differential.name: Cellulitis
differential.why_considered: Erythema, warmth, and swelling around a foot wound are common in both cellulitis and deeper diabetic foot infection.

history: Recent skin break, insect bite, or minor trauma
Pain and redness developing over days
No deep ulcer or exposed bone
exam: Spreading erythema with a defined border
Tenderness limited to the skin and subcutaneous tissue
imaging: No bone or deep soft tissue involvement on imaging

differential.name: Gout or septic arthritis
differential.why_considered: An acutely hot, swollen, painful foot or ankle in a diabetic patient can suggest crystal or joint infection.

history: Sudden onset of severe joint pain over hours
Prior attacks of podagra
No open wound
exam: Severe pain on passive range of motion
labs: Elevated uric acid (may be normal during an attack)
Joint aspirate with monosodium urate crystals
imaging: Joint effusion without bone destruction on plain films

differential.name: Venous stasis ulcer
differential.why_considered: A chronic lower extremity ulcer can occur in diabetic patients with venous insufficiency.

history: Long-standing leg swelling and varicose veins
Ulcer near the medial malleolus
Less pain than an arterial ulcer
labs: No leukocytosis or elevated inflammatory markers

severity.mild: Superficial ulcer limited to the skin or subcutaneous tissue, no signs of infection, adequate perfusion, and the patient is systemically well.
severity.moderate: Ulcer extending to tendon, muscle, or joint with local infection (erythema, warmth, purulent drainage) but no systemic illness.
severity.severe: Deep ulcer with extensive local infection, osteomyelitis, or critical limb ischemia; fever and leukocytosis may be present.
severity.critical: Life-threatening infection such as necrotizing fasciitis or sepsis, or wet gangrene with systemic toxicity requiring urgent surgery.

red_flags.finding: Crepitus, gas in the tissues, or rapidly spreading erythema
red_flags.meaning: Necrotizing soft tissue infection; needs urgent surgical debridement

red_flags.finding: Hypotension, tachycardia, confusion, or elevated lactate
red_flags.meaning: Sepsis or systemic infection; resuscitate and treat emergently

red_flags.finding: Probe-to-bone positive or visible bone in the wound
red_flags.meaning: Osteomyelitis; requires prolonged antibiotics and possible surgical removal of infected bone

red_flags.finding: Absent foot pulses or rest pain
red_flags.meaning: Critical limb ischemia; needs urgent vascular evaluation and revascularization
Tissue necrosis; risk of amputation and systemic spread

red_flags.finding: New fever or chills in a patient with a foot ulcer
red_flags.meaning: Deep or systemic infection until proven otherwise

complications.name: Osteomyelitis
clues: Bone changes on plain films or MRI

complications.name: Necrotizing soft tissue infection
clues: Pain out of proportion to the wound

complications.name: Gangrene
clues: Black, dry or wet necrotic tissue

special_populations.differences: May have a painless, deep ulcer with little or no fever despite serious infection; confusion or falls may be the first sign.
More severe neuropathy and vascular calcification; wounds heal poorly, infection risk is higher, and antibiotic doses need adjustment.
Blunted inflammatory response with minimal redness, warmth, or pus despite deep infection.
Increased plantar pressure and difficulty seeing or reaching the feet, so wounds are found later.
Preexisting or gestational diabetes can accelerate neuropathy and vascular disease; management must balance glycemic control with fetal safety.

key_questions.question: When did you first notice the sore, and how long has it been there?
key_questions.looking_for: Days to weeks or longer; a chronic nonhealing ulcer suggests deep infection or poor perfusion

key_questions.question: Did you feel pain when the wound first appeared?
key_questions.looking_for: Painless or minimally painful wound, indicating loss of protective sensation from neuropathy

key_questions.question: How did the wound start — did you have a blister, cut, callus, or did it appear on its own?
key_questions.looking_for: Minor trauma, ill-fitting shoes, or a callus that broke down; spontaneous ulcer suggests pressure or ischemia

key_questions.question: Is the wound getting bigger, draining, or smelling bad?
key_questions.looking_for: Progression, purulent or foul drainage suggesting infection

key_questions.question: Have you had a foot ulcer or amputation before?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior ulcer or amputation, a strong risk factor for recurrence

key_questions.question: How long have you had diabetes, and what are your recent blood sugar readings or A1c?
key_questions.looking_for: Long-standing diabetes (often more than 10 years) with poor glycemic control

key_questions.question: Do your feet feel numb, tingly, or burning, especially at night?
key_questions.looking_for: Stocking-distribution sensory symptoms of peripheral neuropathy

key_questions.question: Do your legs hurt when you walk and feel better with rest?
key_questions.looking_for: Claudication suggesting peripheral arterial disease and poor perfusion

key_questions.question: Have you had fever, chills, or felt generally unwell?
key_questions.looking_for: Systemic signs suggesting deep or spreading infection

key_questions.question: What do you take for your diabetes, and have you ever taken steroids?
key_questions.looking_for: Insulin or oral agents; steroids worsen hyperglycemia and impair healing

key_questions.question: Do you smoke or use tobacco?
key_questions.looking_for: Tobacco use, which worsens peripheral arterial disease and healing

key_questions.question: Do you check your feet daily, and do you walk barefoot or wear well-fitting shoes?
key_questions.looking_for: Lack of daily foot checks, barefoot walking, or ill-fitting shoes as the cause

key_questions.question: Have you noticed black or dead tissue, or a bad smell from the foot?
key_questions.looking_for: Gangrene or necrotizing infection requiring urgent surgical evaluation

key_questions.question: Is the pain much worse than the wound looks, or is the redness spreading quickly?
key_questions.looking_for: Pain out of proportion or rapidly spreading erythema suggesting necrotizing soft tissue infection

reasoning_points: Long-standing diabetes with peripheral neuropathy causing loss of protective sensation
A painless or minimally painful plantar ulcer over a metatarsal head or the heel, often with surrounding callus
Evidence of peripheral arterial disease such as diminished foot pulses or claudication
Signs of local infection (erythema, warmth, purulent drainage) or systemic infection (fever, leukocytosis)
Probe-to-bone positive or visible bone raising concern for osteomyelitis
Poor glycemic control (elevated glucose and A1c) impairing wound healing
Plain films and MRI used to evaluate for osteomyelitis and Charcot changes
Deep tissue culture rather than a superficial swab to guide antibiotic choice

easy: Long-standing diabetes with classic painless plantar ulcer over a metatarsal head
Obvious loss of protective sensation on monofilament testing
Callus at the ulcer margin and a history of ill-fitting shoes
Elevated glucose and A1c with mild leukocytosis
medium: Ulcer with surrounding cellulitis but no systemic signs
Diminished foot pulses with claudication suggesting coexisting peripheral arterial disease
Probe-to-bone positive with a normal plain film, requiring MRI
Warm, swollen foot where Charcot neuroarthropathy must be distinguished from infection
hard: Older adult with a deep painless ulcer and no fever despite serious infection
Immunocompromised or renal impairment patient with minimal redness or pus
Necrotizing soft tissue infection with pain out of proportion and crepitus
Chronic nonhealing ulcer with osteomyelitis and negative plain films
Wet gangrene with sepsis requiring urgent debridement and amputation discussion
